query: For high-entropy-alloy coatings used in wear-resistant applications, what single intervention could improve wear resistance across operating temperatures? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its expected mechanism, the predicted improvement relative to an otherwise identical unmodified coating, the temperature and sliding conditions under which it should hold, the prior evidence supporting it, and an experiment with a clear result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: The addition of a small amount of yttrium oxide (Y2O3) to high-entropy-alloy (HEA) coatings will improve their wear resistance across operating temperatures.
generation.material_initial_state: High-entropy-alloy coating without yttrium oxide addition
generation.intervention: Addition of 1-2 wt% yttrium oxide (Y2O3) to the HEA coating
generation.conditions: Operating temperatures between 25°C and 500°C, sliding speeds up to 5 m/s, and normal loads up to 1000 N
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of a stable, yttrium-rich oxide layer at the wear surface
generation.mechanism: The Y2O3 addition promotes the formation of a stable, yttrium-rich oxide layer at the wear surface, which reduces adhesive wear and prevents the formation of wear-induced cracks
generation.predicted_outcome: A 20-30% improvement in wear resistance compared to the unmodified HEA coating
generation.boundary: Temperature range: 25°C to 500°C, sliding speed: up to 5 m/s, normal load: up to 1000 N
generation.uncertainty: The optimal amount of Y2O3 addition and the exact mechanism of wear resistance improvement are uncertain and require further investigation

falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the wear volume loss of the Y2O3-modified HEA coating is not significantly lower than that of the unmodified HEA coating at 25°C, 200°C, and 400°C, with a sliding speed of 2 m/s and a normal load of 500 N, then the hypothesis is falsified

cited_evidence.text: ZrC can effectively improve the corrosion resistance of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA coating, and the corrosion resistance of the CrMnFeCoNi HEA coating increases with increasing ZrC content. The annual corrosion rate of the 04ZrC coating in a 1 mol/L NaCl solution is only 21.5% of that of the HEA. Consequently, the addition of ZrC to the FeCoCrNiMn high-entropy alloy coating holds promise for applications in corrosion resistance, particularly in oceanic environments.

One of the most investigated HEA systems is AlCoCrCuFeNi and the copper-free derivate AlCoCrFeNi [,]. Distinct improvement of mechanical properties can be achieved by alloying with titanium. Due to its large atomic radius, the addition of titanium causes solid–solution strengthening and hence increased strength and hardness. Additionally, the formation of brittle phases was observed for a high content of titanium [,,]. The wear resistance of the alloy system AlCoCrFeNiTi has been investigated under various conditions revealing an increased wear resistance, also in comparison with the steels EN 1.3505 and EN 1.3343 [,]. Although improved high-temperature properties of AlCoCrFeNiTi are expected, the wear behaviour has not yet been investigated at increased temperature.

HEA are a class of materials that contain 5–13 principal elements in near-equiatomic proportions; they have attracted a wide range of interesting research due to their excellent mechanical properties []. In recent years, a variety of HEA were reported publicly in the literature [,,,,]. Among them, AlCoCrFeNi HEA composed of a single BCC solid solution phase shows excellent corrosion resistance and has great potential for surface coating applications [,,,,,]. However, an insufficient high temperature wear-resistance of AlCoCrFeNi HEA greatly limits their practical applications at elevated temperatures (above 800 °C). According to the principle of dispersion strength, the strength and hardness of the simple solid solution phases could be improved further by the precipitated intermetallic compound phases. From the perspective of the dispersion strengthening mechanism, WC, TiC ceramic particles are commonly used as reinforcement phases in high-entropy alloys [,,]. These granular-shaped precipitates can improve the microhardness and wear resistance of the coating.
